ai-at-work.title: Hackers are stealing Claude tokens from subscribers
ai-at-work.excerpt: Last month, a Claude user noticed his account was consuming tokens even though he wasn't working. Anthropic has since warned users about hackers.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Someone figured out that their Claude subscription was burning through tokens when they weren't even using it, which led Anthropic to issue a security warning about token theft. This matters because if your AI subscription credentials get compromised, bad actors can run up your bill faster than you can say "unauthorized API call." Here's the thing: people still use the same password for Claude as they do for their email and banking, so this is less a Claude problem and more a "please use a password manager and enable 2FA" wake-up call.

ai-at-work.title: Google Cloud races to catch up in the AI deployment wars with Accenture deal
ai-at-work.excerpt: Google Cloud expands its enterprise AI push with Accenture, betting on forward-deployed engineers to drive adoption and overcome deployment bottlenecks.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Google Cloud signed a deal with Accenture to station engineers inside client organizations, aiming to accelerate enterprise AI implementations and close the gap with AWS and Microsoft. This matters because digital workplace leaders are drowning in AI promises but starving for actual deployment expertise, so having dedicated resources on site could finally turn those pilot projects into real productivity gains. The move is basically Google admitting that selling AI is easy but getting companies to actually use it without blowing up their operations is the hard part, which should tell you everything about where we really are in this cycle.

ai-at-work.title: Chrome is now shipping updates every 2 weeks as AI changes the security landscape
ai-at-work.excerpt: Google is speeding up Chrome’s release schedule to ship security patches and new features faster.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Google is doubling Chrome's update frequency from monthly to every two weeks to address security threats and ship AI-powered features more rapidly. This matters because most organizations manage Chrome deployments, and faster release cycles mean IT teams need tighter testing and approval workflows to keep pace without creating security gaps. The real question is whether your infrastructure can handle this cadence, or if you'll end up running outdated builds because you're still treating browser updates like they're quarterly business reviews.

ai-at-work.title: Meta debuts its ‘secure by design’ personal AI agent Muse
ai-at-work.excerpt: Meta Platforms Inc. is betting that people will be more willing to adopt artificial intelligence agents if they’re simpler to use and they can be trusted. The social media giant today announced Muse,
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Meta launched Muse, a personal AI agent designed to automate digital tasks through a dedicated app with a focus on security and ease of use. For digital workplace folks, this matters because employee adoption of AI tools hinges on trust and simplicity, and Meta's betting that "secure by design" messaging will move the needle on both fronts. Here's the thing though: we've heard the security promise before, and what really drives adoption is whether Muse actually saves people time on work they hate doing, not marketing language about how safe it is.

tools-tech.title: Swiss government explores replacing Microsoft 365 with open-source software
tools-tech.excerpt: Swiss authorities have launched a pilot project to determine whether it is possible to replace Microsoft 365 with similar open-source services, RTS reports. This follows a proof-of-concept project in
tools-tech.dwp_take: Switzerland is running a pilot to ditch Microsoft 365 for open-source alternatives like openDesk, having already tested it with 172 government workers. This matters because if a major government actually pulls off this migration, it proves enterprises can escape vendor lock-in and reclaim some control over their digital infrastructure. Personally, I'll believe it when I see the whole thing running smoothly after year two, but good on them for at least trying what most organizations are too nervous to attempt.

tools-tech.title: Judge spares Google’s ad-tech business from a breakup
tools-tech.excerpt: Back in April 2025, the US Department of Justice (DoJ) proudly proclaimed that it had prevailed in a landmark antitrust case against Google’s ad business. Yeah. Right. You see, just last week, US Dist
tools-tech.dwp_take: A federal judge blocked the Department of Justice's attempt to force Google to divest its AdX ad exchange, effectively gutting what was billed as a landmark antitrust win against the company's ad-tech dominance. This matters to digital workplace pros because Google's ad ecosystem directly affects how organizations buy digital advertising, manage marketing budgets, and compete for visibility online. After years of litigation, the DoJ's "major victory" just became a participation trophy, which tells you everything you need to know about how hard it actually is to rein in tech giants through antitrust action.

tools-tech.title: BigBear 2.0 phishing campaign hijacks Microsoft 365 sessions after MFA
tools-tech.excerpt: A phishing-as-a-service operation targeting Microsoft 365 users has harvested thousands of session cookies that could be used to hijack authenticated sessions after victims complete multifactor authen
tools-tech.dwp_take: Researchers discovered BigBear 2.0, a phishing operation that steals Microsoft 365 session cookies to hijack accounts even after users complete multifactor authentication. This matters because it means MFA alone won't protect your organization if attackers can grab the session token that proves you're already logged in. After three decades watching security theater, I'll say it plainly: if your people are clicking phishing links, no amount of authentication factors will save you from a determined adversary.

digital-culture.title: This ‘union-busting’ calculator arms workers with information
digital-culture.excerpt: When employees dare to organize their workplace, a $1.7 billion industry of consultants and law firms springs into action. According to the Labor Department, something like 75% of employers enlist uni
digital-culture.dwp_take: A startup built a calculator that helps workers understand unionization costs and benefits, directly countering the advice from the 75% of employers dropping millions on union avoidance consultants. This matters because digital workplace professionals often find themselves caught between management directives and employee trust, and transparency tools like this shift the information balance in ways your typical internal comms campaign can't touch. Funny how a spreadsheet can do what millions in consultant fees are designed to prevent, but then again, workers have always been smarter than management gives them credit for.

digital-culture.title: Like working from home? In Australia, it could become the law
digital-culture.excerpt: In some places, the next battle in the war over remote work may be fought in legislatures, not HR departments. The United Kingdom, Ireland, and New Zealand have already passed laws giving workers the
digital-culture.dwp_take: Australia is moving toward legislation that would give workers a legal right to request remote work arrangements, following similar moves in the UK, Ireland, New Zealand, Canada, and the EU. This matters because it signals that employee choice around work location is shifting from a perk HR can revoke to a protected worker right that companies must defend in court. I've watched companies use "return to office" as a cudgel for fifteen years, so watching legislatures basically say "nice try" is genuinely satisfying.

digital-culture.title: Best Workplaces for Innovators 2026: Advertising, marketing, and PR category winners
digital-culture.excerpt: These eight companies stood out to Fast Company’s Best Workplaces for Innovators 2026 judges for enabling employees to innovate with new technologies and effective processes. The integrated PR and mar
digital-culture.dwp_take: Fast Company named eight advertising, marketing, and PR firms as best workplaces for innovation, highlighting companies like Autumn Communications and David&Goliath that invest in employee development and creative processes. For digital workplace pros, this matters because it shows competitive employers are betting on experience design and mobility as retention tools, not just ping pong tables and free coffee. Honestly, a two day bicoastal office swap sounds nice, but let's see if these companies are actually letting people work asynchronously or if innovation just means showing up to a fancier office.

digital-culture.title: Best Workplaces for Innovators 2026: AI, automation, and machine learning excellence category winners
digital-culture.excerpt: From global giants (Google, Lenovo) to household names (Match Group, Williams-Sonoma) to cheekily named upstarts (Kiss My Apps), these 20 companies impressed Fast Company judges with their efforts to

This matters because it signals that investors and media gatekeepers now view technology adoption as a core workplace benefit, not just a cost center play. Here's the thing though: calling yourself innovative on an awards list is easy; actually getting your people to use these tools without losing their minds is the hard part that nobody writes about.

industry-news.title: UN Rights Chief Warns Advanced AI Could Threaten Humanity
industry-news.excerpt: UN rights chief Volker Türk warns advanced AI could threaten humanity without binding safeguards, independent oversight and firm global limits. The post UN Rights Chief Warns Advanced AI Could Threate
industry-news.dwp_take: The UN's top human rights official is raising alarms about advanced AI potentially threatening humanity unless we implement binding safeguards, independent oversight, and global limits on its development. For digital workplace professionals, this matters because we're the ones actually deploying AI tools in production environments right now, and regulation is coming whether we like it or not. Look, I've seen a lot of technology cycles come and go, and the one thing I know for sure is that waiting for perfect global consensus while you're already using AI in your HR systems is a losing strategy.

industry-news.title: Anthropic Walks Away From Reported $6B Decart AI Deal
industry-news.excerpt: Anthropic reportedly ended talks to acquire Decart AI for $6 billion after due diligence, though the companies could still pursue a future partnership. The post Anthropic Walks Away From Reported $6B
industry-news.dwp_take: Anthropic pulled the plug on a reported $6 billion acquisition of Decart AI after getting deep into due diligence, though both sides left the door open for future partnerships instead. This matters because workplace AI tools are consolidating fast, and when major players walk away from expensive deals, it signals either real problems with the target company or a shift in acquisition strategy that affects what tools actually land in your tech stack. Guess even AI companies occasionally remember that throwing billions at a problem doesn't always solve it, which is refreshingly honest compared to most tech industry behavior.

industry-news.title: China Is Turning Its Humanoid Robot Boom Toward the Battlefield
industry-news.excerpt: China’s military is exploring humanoid robots for urban combat as the country’s commercial robotics industry dominates global shipments and manufacturing. The post China Is Turning Its Humanoid Robot
industry-news.dwp_take: China is weaponizing its booming humanoid robot industry by exploring military applications for urban combat scenarios. For digital workplace professionals, this signals a massive acceleration in automation technology that will reshape labor markets and workplace skill requirements faster than most organizations can adapt. Honestly, if your company is still debating whether to invest in basic workplace AI, you're about to get lapped by nations treating robotics like the next arms race, which they kind of are.

industry-news.title: Australia Proposes to Make Social Media Algorithms Optional
industry-news.excerpt: Australia plans to let social media users choose algorithmic or follow-only feeds under new digital safety rules targeting platform design and control. The post Australia Proposes to Make Social Media
industry-news.dwp_take: Australia is proposing new digital safety rules that would let users toggle between algorithmic feeds and chronological follow-only feeds on social media platforms. This matters to digital workplace pros because it signals a regulatory shift toward user control that could reshape how internal social platforms, employee communication tools, and enterprise networks operate if similar rules spread globally. Honestly, it's refreshing to see someone finally ask users what they actually want instead of assuming we all need an algorithm telling us what to think, but watch how quickly platforms find loopholes when forced choice cuts into engagement metrics.
